note.text:
Alkali metals (group 1): soft enough to cut with a knife, shiny when freshly cut, low density (lithium, sodium and potassium float on water). They react with water, giving hydrogen gas and an alkaline solution (sodium + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrogen). They are kept under oil.
Alkaline earth metals (group 2): harder and less reactive than group 1; calcium reacts slowly with water; magnesium burns with a bright white flame.
Halogens (group 7): coloured non-metals, poisonous, made of two-atom molecules (Cl₂). Chlorine is a green-yellow gas used to kill germs in water; iodine is a dark solid used as an antiseptic.
Noble gases (group 8): colourless and very unreactive. Uses: helium in balloons, neon in advertising signs, argon in light bulbs.

worked_example.problem: Why is {m} kept under oil, and what happens when a small piece is put in water?
steps: Sodium reacts quickly with air and water, so it is kept under oil.
In water it floats, moves about, fizzes and gives hydrogen gas; the water becomes alkaline (sodium hydroxide).
worked_example.answer: It reacts with air and water; in water it gives hydrogen and sodium hydroxide.

cards.idea: Alkali metals are soft, light and react with water to give hydrogen and an alkali.
Halogens are coloured, poisonous non-metals made of two-atom molecules.
Noble gases are very unreactive and are used in balloons, signs and bulbs.

pick.q: Why are noble gases used in light bulbs and signs?
pick.y: They do not react with the hot filament.

pick.q: Why is chlorine added to drinking water?
e: Only a little is added, with no colour.

pick.q: Which family reacts with water to give an alkaline solution and hydrogen?
e: Group 2 reacts more slowly; group 1 is the family named for it.
pick.y: Group 1 metals are named for the alkalis they make.
